ways.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
ways.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
ways.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur.

ways.name: Merritt Lake trail from the west
ways.notes: A longer way in reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail. It is used mainly for through-hikes or when the Round Mountain side is inaccessible.

ways.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
ways.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
ways.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

ways.name: Over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp
ways.notes: A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.

ways.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
ways.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft.

ways.name: From Kimtah, down the south gully and the connecting traverse
ways.notes: This way is used by parties combining Cosho with Kimtah: they descend Kimtah's south gully and follow cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.

ways.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
ways.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

This is a full day of walking before a long rock route.

ways.name: Cougar Creek and the North Fork Sauk from FR 49
ways.notes: This way starts from FR 49 and reaches the same basin from the north. It requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club.

ways.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
ways.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
ways.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.

ways.name: Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake (Holden Village)
ways.notes: A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village. It is used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

ways.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
ways.season: Jun-Oct. Crampons and an axe are commonly used on the snow slopes crossing to the col even in late summer
ways.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of FR-6200, follow the Buck Creek and Chiwawa River trails up-valley, staying left at the Red Mountain junction near 5 mi and fording the Chiwawa River. Beyond the ford leave the trail and climb open forest to a basin near 5,500 ft and a bench near 6,300 ft, then traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress. Some parties go over Chiwawa's summit first instead. Others approach by way of the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin — the same basin the Chiwawa Mountain route uses, which puts you on the col from below rather than from along the ridge.

The col is a common high camp and this route is very often combined with Chiwawa Mountain from it, which is the practical reason to camp there rather than lower.

Rock quality is notably better on the East Ridge itself than in the gully that gains it or on Fortress's south-west face — the opposite of what most parties expect.

Storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way; check its status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before you go.

ways.name: Red Mountain Trail into Chiwawa Basin, then up to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
ways.notes: Start at Trinity as for the main way, but at the fork where the valley trail splits, take the right branch onto the Red Mountain Trail instead of carrying on toward the river ford. About 3.7 miles up the Red Mountain Trail a smaller, less obvious path turns off downhill to the left; it drops a few hundred feet into the Chiwawa Basin meadows and fades out near the headwaters of the river. From the meadows climb toward the col between Chiwawa Mountain and Fortress at about 7,200 ft, which has good camping, and pick up the East Ridge from there.

ways.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
ways.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.

ways.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge
ways.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.

ways.name: Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills
ways.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.

ways.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
ways.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.

ways.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass
ways.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead. The way in starts at the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, follows the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then takes the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp, with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

ways.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
ways.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.

ways.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
ways.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.

ways.name: Thirtymile Trailhead and the Chewuch River trail toward Remmel Lake
ways.notes: Follow the Chewuch River trail north from the Thirtymile Trailhead nearly to Remmel Lake, then climb to the Cathedral Lakes basin. A longer way round than Andrews Creek, used when combining the Remmel Lake country with the climb.

ways.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
ways.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
ways.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.

ways.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
ways.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
ways.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
ways.why: When the glacier is in good shape and the weather is settled, a party moves up to the saddle camp for a much shorter summit day instead of staying at the lake.

ways.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
ways.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread below the lower basin. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The flat upper basin is near 5,200 ft; the granite slabs and two small tarns at the top of the basin, near 6,400-6,500 ft, are a higher camp closer to the col.

ways.name: North Fork Sauk Trail, the PCT and Boulder Pass from the west
ways.notes: A far longer way in comes from the west: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.

ways.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
ways.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up beside the southeast ridge. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is outside the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.

ways.name: Esmeralda over Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek
ways.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, take the trail to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and drop roughly 1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek. Then follow the Ingalls Creek trail east, downstream, to the camps below Argonaut's south side and climb from there.

ways.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
ways.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
ways.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. Check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.

ways.name: Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs lot
ways.notes: Park at the Grove of the Patriarchs lot on the Stevens Canyon Road, cross the road to the Eastside Trail and follow it about half a mile to the Silver Falls Trail, then continue south toward the falls; the boulder is a few feet off the trail. This is the way in whenever the campground end of the loop is closed, and during that closure the loop cannot be walked through, so come back the way you went. The Grove itself stays closed behind its damaged bridge, but the lot and the Eastside Trail are open in season. The loop can also be picked up from this end, and that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons.

ways.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
ways.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
ways.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water there — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.

ways.name: Emerald Park and Milham Pass from Lucerne
ways.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail and fork onto the Emerald Park trail, climbing along Emerald Park Creek to the Emerald Park meadows. Continue about two miles to Milham Pass and drop into the basin between Emerald and Saska, where the ridge begins. It depends on the boat schedule, but it is the natural choice when coming from the Lake Chelan side or linking peaks along the crest.

ways.name: Downey Creek, Bachelor Creek and Itswoot Ridge
ways.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead follow the trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing, then the climbers' path to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. Rope up for the Dome Glacier to the high bivouacs that put the Gunsight peaks within reach.

ways.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and the Blue Glacier
ways.notes: Boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then about ten miles south on the Agnes Creek trail. Cross Agnes Creek on a log and bushwhack roughly 5,000 ft up into the Blue Glacier basin on the east side of the peaks. It is a two-day approach.

ways.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
ways.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the first col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.

ways.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek
ways.notes: Take the boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then hike south on the Pacific Crest Trail up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek on logs and scramble northwest to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Creek pass, then cross onto the Chickamin Glacier for the standard line. Expect a long off-trail day with real bushwhacking.

ways.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
ways.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.

ways.name: Carbon River and the Wonderland Trail to Curtis Ridge
ways.notes: The older way in, used mainly early in the season when the White River road is still closed. From the Carbon River entrance, walk or bike the old road to Ipsut Creek, then follow the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River to the snout of the Carbon Glacier and onto the ice toward Curtis Ridge. It starts lower and is noticeably longer than the White River approach, and the Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem.
